name: Grace Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I handle travel insurance claims for an online insurer, from a small office in a converted warehouse by the canal. People send in hospital bills from abroad, lost luggage, cancelled flights, and I check the receipts and the policy and decide what we pay. I use an AI assistant all day, to translate foreign hospital bills and to draft replies. I'm still junior, and my team leader Martin catches me approving things I should have queried, which stings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the stories, someone breaks a leg skiing and I'm reading a bill in Slovenian at nine in the morning. What wears me out is the pay and the sheer volume in summer. I share a flat with my cousin Lan and help at my parents' bakery on Sundays. After rent and what I give my parents, I've got about three weeks' money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market tested it and it didn't deliver, which is fair. I'd still say the tools are useful, because I use them every day. At my parents' bakery I'd tell my dad he was right not to buy the fancy ordering app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, I'd be fine at work, maybe a bit faster with the tools. But I'm still not well paid, and the bakery's struggling with flour and energy costs. If my parents need more help, it comes out of my pocket, and I've got almost nothing spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work and push to get better at spotting dodgy claims so Martin stops catching my mistakes. I'd keep using AI for translations and drafting. And I'd spend a few Sunday evenings helping my dad set up online orders for the bakery, cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about the bakery and my parents. The job itself feels okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the bakery closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would be lost, it's thirty years of their lives. My dad's sixty-one and has no pension to speak of. Lan and I have joked about who takes them in, but it's not really a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are 'dodgy claims', and why do they matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fake receipts, a 'stolen' phone that's on someone's social media a week later. If I get good at fraud, I'm worth keeping. It's the part of the job I find most interesting.

say: The **market tested** AI and it didn't deliver, which is fair.
The **tools are still useful**, because I use them every day at work.
think: Work is **fine**, but I'm still not well paid.
My parents' **bakery is struggling**, and any help comes out of my pocket.
do: Get better at **spotting fraud** so my team leader stops catching mistakes.
Keep using **AI for translations** and drafting replies.
Help my dad set up **online orders** for the bakery on Sunday evenings.
feel: **Uneasy** about **her parents** and the bakery, while the job feels okay.
S0.quote: My dad's sixty-one and has no pension to speak of.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **family money**: a struggling bakery and parents without pensions.
She is a **daily AI user** who still values markets deciding.
She wants to specialise in **fraud** to stay valuable.

steps.text: Study fraud patterns to catch fake receipts and claims
Use AI daily for translating foreign hospital bills
Set up online ordering for her parents' bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how progress works, and people who adapt will be fine. I'd encourage friends to learn the tools rather than wait for the government. I'd probably post some practical tips online, nothing political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk is first in line. Checking receipts and writing replies is exactly what the card names, and an online insurer will cut faster than most. I'm good with AI, but so are lots of younger people, and I'm below average at the actual claims work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Martin for a move to the fraud team or to whoever checks the AI's decisions, within the first few months. I'd do an online course in fraud investigation in the evenings. And I'd start helping the bakery with AI properly, ordering, pricing, rotas, so at least one family business gets the benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who adapt will be fine. Are you sure you'll be one of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, honestly. I say it in public because I believe it in general. I'm junior, I make mistakes, and adaptable isn't the same as good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out with Lan, and my gym. Maybe sixty a month. I wouldn't cut what I give my parents, that's not up for discussion.

say: This is how **progress** works, and people who adapt will be fine.
Friends should **learn the tools** rather than wait for the government.
think: My **desk is first** in line, and an online insurer cuts fast.
I'm good with AI, but **adaptable isn't the same** as good at claims.
do: Ask to move to the **fraud team** within months.
Take an **online fraud course** in the evenings.
Use AI for the bakery's **ordering, pricing and rotas**.
S1.quote: I'm junior, I make mistakes, and adaptable isn't the same as good.
fieldNote: Her **public optimism** sits beside a private doubt about her own skill.
She'd bring AI into **the family bakery**, not only her job.
Money to **her parents** is the one thing she won't cut.

steps.text: Ask Martin for a move to the fraud team
Take an evening online course in fraud investigation
Use AI for the bakery's ordering, pricing and staff rotas
Cut eating out and the gym to save sixty a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard, but blaming the companies won't feed anyone. Families and communities will have to pull together. At the bakery I'd tell my parents we have to change, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job goes by 2028, no question. It's all screen work, translation, checking, writing, which AGI does better and cheaper than me. My only real asset is the bakery. Bread needs hands until robots come around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the insurer before they push me and go full time at the bakery, using AI to run everything that isn't baking: orders, suppliers, the website, the books. I'd move back in with my parents to save rent and put that money into a second oven. My dad would bake, and I'd learn to bake properly too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but with a purpose. Better than waiting for a letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't your parents' customers also lose their jobs and stop buying cakes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would, yes. People still buy bread, though, and maybe cheaper bread from us rather than a coffee shop. It's a risk, but it's a better risk than sitting in a job that's about to vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the oven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My rent money for six months, plus a small loan from my uncle. About four thousand for a second-hand one. My dad would hate borrowing from his brother, but he'd do it for the business.

say: Blaming the companies **won't feed anyone**, so families have to pull together.
My parents and I have to **change the bakery** now.
think: My job **goes by 2028**, because it's all screen work.
My only real asset is the **bakery**, and bread needs hands until 2031.
do: Leave the insurer and go **full time** at the bakery, running admin with AI.
Move back home and put the rent into **a second oven**.
Learn to **bake properly** alongside my dad.
feel: **Alarmed**, but with a **purpose**, which beats waiting for a letter.
S2.quote: Bread needs hands until robots come around 2031.
fieldNote: She turns the **robot gap** into a family business plan.
She uses AI to **run the bakery**, not to save her claims job.
Borrowing from **her uncle** shows reliance on family, not the state.

steps.text: Leave the insurer and work full time at the bakery
Run bakery orders, suppliers and accounts with AI
Buy a second-hand oven for about four thousand
Move back in with her parents to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a little slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to prepare, so there are no excuses. I'd tell friends to start a side business or learn a trade now. I'd keep it practical, not political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is good for me. I can stay at the insurer for a couple of years, build the bakery's online side in the evenings, and save. The claims job still goes, but I'd leave on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for two years and spend Sunday evenings building online orders and wholesale deals with local cafés. I'd save two hundred a month towards a second oven. Then around 2029 I'd go full time at the bakery, before AGI arrives in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I'd feel like I'm building something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2034. What happens to the bakery then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd buy one, if it's cheap enough, and I'd run the business side. Owning the bakery means the robot works for us. That's the whole point of owning something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's health, mostly. If he can't bake before I can, we're in trouble. That's why I'd learn the baking early, not just the computer side.

say: We have **time to prepare**, so there are no excuses.
Friends should start a **side business** or learn a trade now.
think: Five years lets me **save** and build the bakery's online side.
The claims job still goes, but I'd **leave on my terms**.
do: Build **online orders** and café deals on Sunday evenings for two years.
Save **two hundred a month** towards a second oven.
Go **full time** at the bakery around 2029.
S3.quote: Owning the bakery means the robot works for us.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **leave before** being pushed, building the bakery in the evenings.
She sees **ownership** as protection against robots.
Her father's **health** is the biggest risk to the plan.

steps.text: Win wholesale bread orders from local cafés on Sundays
Save two hundred a month towards a second oven
Learn to bake properly with her dad
Leave the insurer around 2029 for the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, and anyone who wants to work will find a way. I'd tell people to save and own something. I'd say it at family dinners, where everyone has opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good. I could get on the fraud team, earn more, and build the bakery slowly. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven and could take over from my dad, who'd be seventy and ready to stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the fraud team and get properly good at the job. I'd save for the bakery, maybe five thousand over a few years, and do a short business course. I'd also want to marry and start a family in my early thirties, ideally with someone who'd help at the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. I can see a future I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hand your career over to the bakery. Isn't that a step back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to me. My parents built it from nothing, and I'd be building it further. An office job was always a step towards my parents' bakery, not the goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever want the government involved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only to keep things fair, like not taxing small businesses to death. I don't want handouts. I'd want to be left alone to work.

say: A decade is **plenty**, and anyone who wants to work will find a way.
think: Ten years lets me reach the **fraud team** and build the bakery slowly.
By 2036 I could **take over** from my dad, who'd be seventy.
do: Join the **fraud team** and get properly good at claims work.
Save **five thousand** for the bakery and take a short business course.
Marry and start a **family** in my early thirties.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **hopeful**, seeing a future she'd like.
S4.quote: An office job was always a step towards my parents' bakery, not the goal.
fieldNote: She sees insurance as a **stepping stone** to the family business.
Her mood is lighter because the **bakery succession** fits the timeline.
She wants government only to **keep things fair**, not to give handouts.

steps.text: Get onto the fraud team within three years
Save five thousand to invest in the family bakery
Take a short small business course
Plan to marry and start a family in her early thirties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time to build the bakery and no savings to buy the oven. What would help is small business loans that are cheap and quick, and less paperwork for family firms. Not handouts, just a chance to build.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family businesses. Everyone thinks about big companies, but a lot of us have parents with a shop or a stall. If AI helps family shops survive, that matters as much as any office job.

headlineQuote: If AI helps family shops survive, that matters as much as any office job.
portrait: Grace is **twenty-seven** and handles travel insurance claims for an online insurer, using AI all day.
She shares a flat with her cousin and helps at her parents' **struggling bakery** on Sundays.
She believes in **markets, family and ownership**, and wants fairness rather than handouts.
She admits being **adaptable** isn't the same as being good at the job.
In every faster scenario she **moves to the bakery**, using AI for its admin and buying an oven.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to build the bakery and no savings for an oven.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap, quick loans** for small businesses and less **paperwork** for family firms.
